Note::to_nfc¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::to_nfc() const

Compose Every Cell To Unicode Normalization Form C¶

to_nfc() returns a new Note, same shape as the input, with each cell converted to NFC — the canonical composed form. Where a base letter and its combining marks can be written as one precomposed character, NFC uses the single character: e + U+0301 (combining acute) becomes the single code point é (U+00E9).

NFC is the form the web and most systems expect, and the one to normalise to before storing text, comparing strings byte-for-byte, or computing a hash — two visually identical strings that differ only in composition compare equal after both are put through to_nfc(). It does not change how the text renders, only its bytes, so pair it with lengths_bytes or lengths_chars to see the effect.

to_nfc is shape-preserving, cell-independent, idempotent, and returns a fresh Note. Requires the Unicode backend.

Example 1: A Decomposed Accent Is Composed¶

const std::string decomposed = std::string("caf") + "e\xCC\x81";  // "e" + U+0301
const pluss::Note n = pluss::make_note({decomposed, "abc"}).to_nfc();
std::cout << pluss::note::print(n) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["café", "abc"]

The render is unchanged; the bytes are not.

Example 2: The Byte Count Shows The Change¶

const std::string decomposed = std::string("caf") + "e\xCC\x81";
const auto in = pluss::make_note({decomposed, "abc"});

const auto before = in.lengths_bytes();
const auto after = in.to_nfc().lengths_bytes();
std::cout << "[" << before[0] << ", " << before[1] << "] -> ["
          << after[0] << ", " << after[1] << "]\n";

Output¶

[6, 3] -> [5, 3]

"café" drops from 6 bytes (c a f e + 2-byte combining mark) to 5 (c a f

  • 2-byte precomposed é); the ASCII cell is untouched.
